Know that every voluntary movement has a sequence of sources. The nearest is the power that directly moves the body. In an animal, this power is in the muscle of the limb being moved. Before it comes resolve, then desire, and before desire come thought and imagination. When an image of something appears in the imagination or the intellect, the image itself stirs desire and leads it toward resolve, without any prior decision. The First Agent brings things into existence in a similar way, as will become clear later, God willing: the vision of the highest order causes things to proceed from Him, without desire or the use of an instrument.

Once desire has stirred and resolve is in place, the moving power in the limbs carries it out. This shows that voluntary movements take shape through the sources just described. Sometimes the image formed in the mind is itself the goal at which movement ends. For example, someone grows tired of where they are, imagines another place, longs to be there, and moves toward it. Sometimes the image is not itself the goal: someone may want to go somewhere in order to meet a friend. In the first case, the destination itself is what the person wants. In the second, the desired meeting comes about only after the movement ends. Sometimes the movement itself is what the mover seeks.

It is now clear that the point a movement reaches is its immediate moving power’s primary and true goal. In an animal, that power is in the muscle, and the endpoint is its only goal of its own. The earlier sources of movement may have other goals, as we have seen. If the immediate moving power and the two sources before it—the power of desire, and the thought or image that stirred it—are all directed toward the same goal, then the movement’s endpoint serves them all. The action is not aimless, because it is guided by a deliberate goal. But if the endpoint matches what imagination and desire seek, while failing to match what deliberate thought seeks, the action is aimless.

Any goal that is not the endpoint of a movement, and whose source is not deliberate thought, must come from one of three sources. It may come from imagination alone; then the action is arbitrary. It may come from imagination working with nature or bodily temperament, as in breathing or the movements of a sick person; then the action is natural or necessary. Or it may come from imagination working with a settled trait or habit that prompts action without thought, as when someone plays with their beard; then the action is a habit. When a goal sought by one of these sources does not come about, the action is fruitless in relation to that goal.

With these points in place, we can see that aimless action still has a goal: it is the goal of the power of imagination, as just described. So it is wrong to say that such action has no goal at all, or no goal that is good or thought to be good. An action need not have a goal in relation to a source that did not bring it about; it needs a goal only in relation to the source that did. In aimless action there is no source based on deliberate thought, and so there is no goal of that kind. The other sources, however, each have a goal in the action they cause, and that goal is good in relation to them.

Every action of the soul involves desire and imagination, even if the image that stirred desire does not remain. A person may no longer be aware of it: imagining something and being aware that one is imagining it are not the same. If every awareness required another awareness of itself, this would go on without end. So the desire that arises in someone who is asleep or distracted, or in someone playing with their beard, must have a cause. It may be habit, impatience with one’s present state, a wish to move into another state, or the senses’ urge for some new activity. Habit is pleasurable; so is moving away from a tiresome state, and so is seeking a new activity. Pleasure is a good for the senses or the imagination. It is a real good for an animal as an animal, though from the standpoint of human reason it is only an apparent good. So the action is not without a real good in relation to the source that produced it, even if that good is not a true rational good.

Democritus claimed that the world came about by chance. He said its basic building blocks were tiny bodies, too hard to be split apart. They were scattered through an endless empty space. They all had the same basic nature, but different shapes, and they were always moving. By chance, some collided and came together in a particular arrangement, forming this world. But Democritus did not claim that plants and animals arose by chance. Empedocles, by contrast, claimed that the basic elemental bodies came into being by chance. Whatever arrangement allowed them to survive and reproduce remained; whatever did not, disappeared. He offered several arguments for this view. One was that nature cannot think things through, so how can it act toward a goal?

Another argument was that decay, death, deformities, and extra parts are not intended by nature, even though they follow a steady order, just as their opposites do. This seems to show that none of these outcomes is intended by nature. Withering runs in the opposite direction from growth, but it too follows a fixed pattern. Since withering happens because matter requires it, not because nature intends it, perhaps growth happens for the same reason: matter requires it, without nature planning or aiming for it.

Rain is an example. The sun turns water into vapor. The vapor reaches a cold region, cools, becomes heavy water, and must fall. Sometimes the rain happens to be useful, so people think it was meant to bring those benefits. But, this argument says, rain falls because matter requires it.

A third argument was that the same natural power can produce different results. Heat melts wax, hardens salt, darkens a laundry worker’s face, and whitens clothes. These are the arguments made by those who say things happen by chance. Before answering them, we need to set out a few points.

Some possible events happen every time; others happen most of the time. Each has a cause. The difference is that nothing interferes with an event that always happens, while an event that happens most of the time can be blocked. It happens when no obstacle gets in the way, whether it comes about naturally or by choice. For a person to carry out an intended action, they must be resolved, their body must be ready to move, no obstacle can block the movement, they must not change their mind, and they must be able to reach the goal. Given these conditions, they cannot fail to reach it.

Other events happen just as often as their opposites, like Zayd sitting down or standing up. Some happen only rarely, like a person having an extra finger. We do not call events that always happen or happen most of the time “chance.” The other two cases—events that happen equally often and events that are rare—can be necessary under certain conditions.

For example, while an embryo’s hand is forming, more material may remain than is needed for its five fingers. If the active power then finds the material fully ready, an extra finger must form. Given those conditions, the extra finger forms necessarily. Relative to this particular natural process, it is as regular as any other result, even though it is rare among members of the species.

Once we see that even rare events are certain when their causes and conditions are present, there is no doubt that equally likely events can become common or regular when we take their causes and conditions into account. What happens by chance does so only for people who do not know its causes. From the standpoint of the one who sets all causes in motion, with every surrounding cause taken into account, nothing happens by chance. As the philosophers say, every event is necessary once all its causes are in place. If a person knew every cause and condition, nothing would seem to happen by chance.

If someone digging a well finds a treasure, that is chance only to someone who does not know what led the digger to that spot or brought the treasure to light. To someone who knows all the causes, the discovery is not chance but necessary.

Even a chance event happens through a process that has its own goal. It is only an incidental result of that process, not its main goal. Sometimes a falling stone injures someone, then continues down to its natural resting place, which is the proper goal of its movement. Sometimes it injures someone and stops before reaching that place. In the first case, it reaches its natural goal, while the injury is incidental. In the second, it fails to reach its natural goal.

Chance, then, is an incidental outcome of a natural, chosen, or forced process. Those processes already have their own goals; without them, nothing could happen by chance. Chance enters when an unexpected event occurs, one that does not happen always or most of the time. Still, the process must be capable of leading to that outcome, at least occasionally; otherwise we would not call it chance.

For example, if a solar eclipse happens while Zayd is sitting down, we would not call his sitting a chance cause of the eclipse: sitting has nothing to do with bringing about an eclipse. But when we trace an event back to the causes that truly bring it about, we find that it has a natural or chosen goal of its own. So the world did not come into being by chance, though chance may play a part in some individual events. The claims made by Empedocles and Democritus are false.

Here is the detailed answer to the objections. First, the fact that nature cannot think things through does not mean that its actions have no goal. Thought does not give an action its goal; it helps choose one action from among several possible actions. Each action has its own goal by nature, and reaches it without anyone having to assign it that goal. If the soul had no competing motives or distractions, people would act in one steady way without thinking, as the heavenly spheres do. They are free of changing urges and disturbances, so their actions follow a constant pattern without thought.

Another point supports the claim that nature acts toward goals: reasoning itself is an action with a goal, yet it does not need another act of reasoning to guide it. It is also clear that crafts have goals. Once a skill becomes a habit, a person can use it without thinking through each step. In fact, thinking about every step can get in the way. A skilled writer does not stop to consider each letter, and a skilled musician does not think about each note. If they did, their skill would suffer. So nature, too, can act toward goals without thought or planning.

The same is true when someone slips and grabs whatever they can to keep from falling, or when a hand moves to scratch an itch without thought. Even clearer: when the soul moves an arm or leg, it does so through a tendon, though the soul is not aware of the tendon.

In reply to the second objection: things sometimes break down because they lack what they need to reach their full form, and sometimes because an obstacle or outside influence interrupts nature’s course. As for these absences, nature’s being directed toward a goal does not mean it must always reach it. Death, decay, and withering happen because natural processes fall short of their intended goal. There is a deeper point here that I cannot explain in this section.

Withering also follows a goal. It has two causes: heat, which acts directly, and the body’s nature, which contributes indirectly. Each has its own goal. Heat draws out moisture, drives the material toward that result, and uses it up in an orderly way. The body’s nature, by contrast, tries to preserve the body for as long as it can by drawing on one supply after another. But each new supply is smaller than the last, as we will explain in the discussion of the soul. The shrinking supply leads indirectly to the orderly process of withering; the loss of moisture leads to it directly. Each process has its own goal.

Death may not be a goal for one particular body, but it serves the wider order that prepares the soul for eternal life. The same is true of bodily weakness and aging: the soul is disciplined through them, and its bodily powers are weakened in ways that prepare it for the next life, as we will explain in the discussion of the soul.

Extra parts also arise for a reason. When there is more matter than the body needs, nature gives it the form it is ready to receive instead of leaving it unused. So nature acts toward a goal in producing an extra part, even if that part does not serve the body as a whole. We have not claimed that every goal of nature must serve the whole body.

The argument about rain is also mistaken. Rain comes from heavenly arrangements meeting receptive conditions on earth. Together, these serve the order of the whole world and bring good and blessings. They are causes from God, and nature brings them about always or most of the time.

In reply to the third objection: heat has one proper goal—to make the thing it heats take on a nature like its own. Its other effects, such as melting, hardening, darkening, and whitening, are necessary side effects. Later, we will see how a side effect can also serve as an indirect goal.

In The Healing, Ibn Sina gives arguments against Empedocles’ view, based on observation and clear examples. Some readers have therefore thought Empedocles’ remarks about chance and fortune were symbolic, or were falsely attributed to him. They say this because the other works they read show sound reasoning and great learning.

One clear example is this: if a grain of wheat and a grain of barley fall in the same patch of soil, the wheat grows into wheat and the barley into barley. This shows that the power in each seed makes the nearby soil take the form of that plant. It is not simply a result of matter’s needs, since the soil is much the same in both places. Even if the parts of the soil differed, they would not differ because of the nature of earth itself. The power in the seed gives that part of the soil its special quality. If the seed’s power got this quality from an earlier quality, the chain would go on forever. If it did not, then the power in the wheat seed is naturally directed toward a particular goal. Otherwise, why would an olive tree not grow from wheat, or barley from a watermelon seed?

Another point is that the goals nature reaches when nothing blocks it are all good and complete. When nature produces the opposite, that happens only rarely. This is why people look for some outside cause and ask: “What happened to this animal that made it sick and weak? Why did wheat or barley fail to grow?” Nature, then, is directed toward what is good whenever nothing stands in its way. When we see nature falling short, we help it through skill, as a doctor does. The doctor believes that once the obstacle is removed and nature’s power grows stronger, nature will bring about health and good. This supports the point.
Section 3 — The Goals of Chosen Actions

Some people who deny God’s attributes say that God’s actions serve no wisdom or good purpose. Yet you have seen that nature acts toward goals, and that even the actions of people who are asleep or distracted serve the needs of some power within them—the power that actually causes the action—even when reason or thought does not guide it. These people rely on arguments weaker than a spider’s web. For example, they try to show that actions need no motive by pointing to two equal roads for a person fleeing, two equal loaves for someone hungry, or two equal cups of water for someone thirsty. They do not realize that our failure to see what tips the balance does not prove that there is no such cause. Some of the things that guide our actions are hidden from us, such as the positions of the stars and higher divine causes.

They also fail to see that if we deny motives for action and allow choices to happen without any reason, we close the way to proving that there is a Creator. The proof begins from this point: something that could exist or not exist needs a cause that makes one outcome happen. If we reject this rule, we cannot prove that God must exist. And if we accept their view, there is no firm basis for thought or inquiry, or even for trusting what is plainly true, because we could never be sure that the opposite of a conclusion would not follow. Their view could even make God create in a person a state that makes things appear other than they are, since they say God can will without any reason. In Muslim history, these people resemble the ancient Sophists.

Another argument is that will itself tips the balance between alternatives, as an essential feature of will. Essential features and what belongs to a thing’s nature need no further explanation, just as knowledge is knowledge and power is power. But this is empty talk. If the two possible actions are equal, what makes one happen rather than the other? The special feature they appeal to is nonsense: it would still be there if, as they suppose, the other equally possible action had been chosen.

Another claim they repeat is that will exists before an action without being directed toward anything in particular, and then becomes directed toward one thing rather than another. This alone shows the weakness of their view. Someone who wills does not simply will whatever happens to come along. Will is a relation, so it cannot exist without being directed toward something; it cannot first exist on its own and only later attach itself to one thing. Rather, when we imagine something before it exists and one side of its possibility is favored, a will directed toward that side arises. The preference comes before the will, as we have said. The strongest arguments they offer are points raised by the author of The Eastern Investigations.

First, a heavenly sphere is a body whose parts are alike, yet two points in it are singled out as its poles, one circle as its equator, and one line as its axis. Since every point, circle, and line is alike in nature, the poles, equator, and axis could have been elsewhere.

Second, each sphere moves in a particular direction, though it could move in any direction. Each also moves at a particular speed, though it could move faster or slower and either option seems equally possible.

Third, each planet occupies a particular place in its sphere, though nothing in that place makes it different from the others. Since all places have the same nature, reason allows that the planet could have been somewhere else.
Fourth, the universe has a particular size rather than being larger or smaller, though either seems possible to reason.

The answer to the first point is that the point became special through the particular motion. That motion sets the two poles; once they are set, the axis between them is set as well. Without the motion, no circle would be fixed as the equator, and so no pole or axis would be fixed.

The answer to the second point is that differences in the spheres’ directions and speeds follow from differences in their intellectual principles, which cause the spheres and their motions in a way that brings about the best order.

This also answers the third point. A planet’s place became definite through the planet itself, not before it existed; otherwise, the sphere would be solid, with no place for the planet. Once the planet exists in that place, it cannot move to another.

As for the fourth point, every body, including the outermost sphere, has a nature that requires it to have a particular size. It cannot be otherwise. What reason allows us to imagine may not match reality, because before a proof we may not know the specific feature that makes the cause produce this result. I have a separate treatise on these problems, where I set out basic principles that remove doubt. Anyone seeking reassurance should consult it.

In short, if an agent has only a possible relation to an effect and no motive or cause that leads it to act, the effect cannot come from it. One of two equal possibilities cannot become more likely than the other. A rational person who says otherwise is only saying the words, not believing them. This motivating purpose is the goal of bringing things into existence. For God, that goal is His own essence, because He is a complete agent. If He needed something outside Himself in order to act, He would not be complete in His agency. You will see that He is the cause of all causes, and that His action has no ultimate goal beyond Himself.

Goals, like all other causes, depend on Him. If His action had a goal beyond Himself, then either that goal would not depend on Him—which contradicts what we have assumed—or it would depend on Him. In that case, we would ask again what goal led Him to bring about that goal, and continue in the same way until we reached a goal that is His own essence. His essence, then, is the goal of all things, just as He is their cause.

We will show, God willing, that the Necessary Existent takes the greatest joy in His own essence, and that His essence is the source of all things. Whoever takes joy in something also takes joy in what comes from it, insofar as it comes from that thing. God wills things not for their own sake, considered by themselves, but because they come from His essence. The goal of His creation of the world is His own sacred essence. Any agent whose action follows this pattern is both the agent and the goal of that action. Even if pleasure in us were aware of itself, and its own essence were the source of an action, it would will that action for its own sake and because the action came from it. It would then be both agent and goal.

They often say that what is higher does not will or attend to what is lower. If it did, it would be perfected by what is lower, since that thing’s existence would be better for it than its absence; but a cause is not perfected by its effect. This does not undermine our argument. What is denied is direct love and attention, aimed at the lower thing for its own sake—not love that follows as a consequence. If God loves and wills His action because it is an effect of His essence, a trace of His outpouring and existence, it does not follow that this action is itself a source of goodness or joy for Him. His joy is in what He loves directly: His exalted essence, from which every perfection and beauty flows.

It is said that a reader once recited before Abu Saʿid ibn Abi al-Khayr, may God have mercy on him, the verse “He loves them, and they love Him.” The master replied: “God loves them because He loves only Himself. Nothing exists but Him; all else is His work. When a maker praises his work, he praises himself.”

This makes clear what is meant by the saying: “Were it not for love, neither heaven nor earth, land nor sea would exist.” God’s love for creation returns to Him. In truth, what He loves and wills is His own essence, for its own sake. It is like loving a person and then loving the traces he has left: the true object of your love is that person, as the poet says:
It was not love of the houses that captured my heart, but love of the one who lived in them.
Section 4 — The Purpose of Beings That Follow One Another Without End

Before we explain this, we need to make one point clear. Some outcomes are not the main goal, but are necessary along the way. They come in three kinds. The first is something that must exist before the main goal can be reached. For example, iron must be hard for cutting to work. This is called useful, either in fact or only in our estimation. Death and similar things belong here. Death serves the order of living things as a whole, and the soul too, as we have mentioned.

The second kind is something that must accompany what the goal depends on. For example, cutting requires an iron knife, which may be dark. The darkness is not needed for cutting; it simply comes with the iron that is needed.

The third kind comes after the main goal. It may follow necessarily, as earthly events follow the motions of the heavenly spheres, whose goal is something higher than the motions themselves. Or it may not follow necessarily, as a parent’s love for a child may follow marriage, whose goal is having children. All three kinds are indirect goals, also called necessary outcomes. The evil we find in our world belongs to this last kind of necessary outcome. Divine providence, which is generosity, requires that every good exist. That includes the elements that combine to form other things. But fire cannot exist without having the power to burn, and the order of the world depends on fire serving its proper role. So some of the things made from these elements are destroyed. The motions of the heavenly spheres, which follow divine governance and the order it requires, bring fire to the things it destroys. What is necessary in each instance of evil serves a goal in relation to something else or to the order of the whole, as we saw in the discussion of good. We will explain this further when we discuss divine providence, God willing.

Once this is clear, we can say that the proper goal of the natural power that governs the world is not the continued existence of one particular individual of a kind. Its proper goal is for each kind to continue to exist. If one individual can last, then there is no need for individuals to replace one another; only one individual exists, as with the sun and moon. But if one individual cannot last, as with things that come to be and perish, then new individuals must follow one another. This series of individuals is not wanted for its own sake. It is needed because the proper goal cannot be reached without it. So the endless succession of individuals is an incidental goal, not a true goal in itself. True goals are finite.

That is the goal of the natural power that guides each kind. An individual’s nature aims to preserve that individual; it has no other goal. As for the unbroken motion of the heavenly sphere, its purpose, as you will learn, is to bring every possible arrangement into reality, so that the souls of the spheres can become more like what is perfect. This can happen only through a succession of particular arrangements. So those changing arrangements are incidental goals, like the earthly events mentioned above.

As for the reasons and conclusions in an argument, the claim that a goal must be finite means that one agent cannot pursue one goal, then another, and another without end in a single action. It does not mean that many actions cannot have many goals. Each argument has its own conclusion, and in following it the mind seeks only that conclusion. There is no problem here.
Chapter 23 — The Difference Between a Goal and a Good

A goal may lie within the created world, or it may be above it. If it lies within the created world, it may exist in what receives it—for example, the shape of a house in the clay and bricks a builder uses—or it may exist in the agent’s own mind, as the shelter the builder hopes to provide. In every case, the final cause—the goal toward which an action is directed—is the first cause on which the other causes depend. Unless an agent first pictures a goal, it cannot act. Yet when a goal exists in the outside world, it is itself brought about by the other causes.

Consider first the kind of goal that exists in what receives it. In relation to the agent, when the agent imagines it and is moved to act by that thought, it is the purpose. In relation to movement, it is an endpoint, not a purpose: a thing is completed when it reaches its goal and remains once reached, while movement ends when it reaches its endpoint. In relation to the agent’s being completed by it—when the agent could not yet do something but becomes able to do it—it is a good. Whatever brings a possibility to completion is a perfection; absence is bad. So attaining something and bringing it into reality are good.

When we consider the goal in relation to what receives it, and how that thing becomes what it is through the goal, the goal is its form. The goal that exists in the agent is a form or quality within the agent. If we consider it as something that completes the agent, it is a good; if we consider it as what starts the agent’s movement, it is a goal. So every goal is a goal in one respect and a good in another, either truly good or only thought to be good. This applies, for example, to some actions prompted by imagination alone, without careful thought or natural impulse.

You should also know that the goal of an agent that directly acts on matter is a form within that matter. An agent whose goal is not a form within matter is not acting directly on it. Sometimes the same person acts both directly and indirectly, and in different roles: close to the material or farther away, directly shaping it or not. In that case, the form made in the material is the person’s goal in one way directly and in another way as a side effect.

For example, someone builds a house to live in. As someone seeking shelter, he is the prior cause of the building: his wish to live there leads him to build. As the builder, he acts because he seeks shelter. From the builder’s point of view, the goal is something beyond the house’s shape; but in the role of directly shaping the material, his goal is the house’s form and structure.
Chapter 24 — The Difference Between Good and Generosity

A goal may move an agent to act, and so be the purpose of its action. In another sense, the goal is something brought about by the action. In this second sense, we can ask how it relates to the agent that is completed by it and to the agent that produces it. If the result does not affect the agent or anything that depends on it, what it brings about is simply existence. If the agent is changed or improved by the result, what it receives is a good. In general, good is what every thing seeks: existence, or a fuller existence.

Generosity means giving what is fitting without asking for anything in return. Someone who gives what does not suit the receiver is not generous—for example, giving a knife to someone who plans to kill an innocent person. Nor is someone generous if they give a benefit in order to receive something back, whether thanks, praise, a good name, or pleasure. A generous agent gives another being a perfection in its nature or circumstances without receiving anything in return.

So an agent who acts for a goal that serves as a kind of repayment is not generous. That agent is making a deal and expecting something back. This makes the agent incomplete and needy: it gives one thing to gain something better and more pleasant for itself. If an agent ought to do something but does not, it lacks a perfection and is incomplete. If its perfection depends on something else, it is needy—even if that other thing completes someone else, removes their need, or brings them good.

If another’s good and the agent’s own gain or loss matter equally to the agent, there is no reason for it to bring good to the other. Its action remains only a possibility, because an aim is what moves an agent to act; something that does not tip the balance is not an aim. If the two do not matter equally, the explanation eventually returns to something connected to the agent itself. The question “Why?” keeps coming back until it reaches the agent’s own nature—some good it gains or some harm it avoids. Then the questioning stops. Every thing seeks its own good and the removal of what harms it. An agent acts from love of what it values, and each thing seeks what it values most: itself. So anyone who acts to gain something is incomplete; in short, they seek something they do not have. This is the view we find in their books.

Further comment and clarification: The study of goals is truly part of wisdom, and perhaps its best part. But books on the subject contain loose statements and claims that have not been fully worked out. These can be settled only by careful discussion and deep study. We should examine them closely and answer the doubts they raise as far as we can.

If you look carefully at a goal, you will find that it is always the same as the cause that acts. The difference lies in how we view it. For example, when a hungry person eats to become full, he eats because he pictures being full. He tries to bring that fullness about in reality, moving from imagining it to having it. As he imagines being full, he is the one who eats so that he can become full in fact. The imagined fullness completes the cause that makes him act; actual fullness is the goal that follows from the action. Eating thus comes from fullness and brings about fullness, but in two different senses. As an idea in the mind, fullness is the cause that makes him act; as a reality, it is the goal. The goal in the agent’s mind is never separate from the agent, and the result of the action also returns to the agent by completing it.

This shows why the usual divisions of goals do not hold. They say a goal may be in the agent, as joy is; in what receives the action; or in someone else, as another person’s approval. But the last two kinds really return to the first. A builder does not build, and someone does not win another person’s approval, unless some benefit comes back to them. This is true whether “goal” means what moves the agent to act or what naturally follows from the action.

They also say that a goal may be the very place where a movement ends, or something else—for example, moving to escape boredom with one place or to meet a friend. But unless the agent sees one option as better, or seeks some happiness or benefit that returns to them, voluntary movement could not happen.

We can make sense of this last distinction, but not by saying, as some do, that in both lists “goal” simply means the endpoint produced by an action. As we have already seen, even that endpoint must bring some good back to the agent, at least as the agent imagines it, if nothing blocks the result. Rather, the distinction is about what the goal is in itself: either the very thing at which movement ends, or something else.

The philosophers say that God’s actions are not done for aims or goals. Yet they often call Him the “goal of goals” and say that He is both the beginning and the end. The Qur'an says that all things return to God, and that the return is to Him, among many other such statements. If saying that God’s actions have no goal means that they are not directed toward anything outside His own essence, that is true. As we said earlier, the First Cause is complete in His agency and does not depend on anything else in order to act. But that does not mean that His action has no goal or purpose at all. We may understand His knowledge of the good order—which is identical with His essence—as the purpose and goal of creation.

If you say, “The final cause, as the philosophers explicitly state, is what makes an agent act. It must therefore be different from the agent itself, since what brings something about must differ from what it brings about,” I reply: The philosophers often use words such as “requires” loosely. They may use them simply to mean that one thing cannot be separated from another. How else could they claim that an agent and its goal must be different in reality without proving it?

An agent is what gives existence; a goal is that for whose sake existence is given. The goal may be the agent’s own essence, or something higher than it. If the goal were something that exists in its own right and produces an action from its own nature, it would be both the one acting and the goal.

So when the philosophers deny that God acts for a goal, they mean a goal separate from His own essence: honor, praise, thanks, bringing benefit to someone else, or any other result of His action that does not enter into His purpose. But if we mean that His knowledge of the good order—which is identical with His essence—gives rise to His bringing good into being, then careful inquiry and proof lead us to affirm this. The greatest minds have recognized it.

Avicenna states this in his Notes: “If someone knew the perfection that is the Necessary Existent by itself, then arranged all the things that come after it according to its pattern so that they reached the highest order, that person would truly have aimed at the Necessary Existent by itself, which is perfection. If the Necessary Existent by itself is the agent, then it is also the goal.”

We have said that the First Principle is the goal of things in this sense. He is also their goal because every thing seeks its own perfection and, as far as it can, tries to resemble Him in attaining it. Each has a love and longing for Him, whether by choice or by nature. The philosophers who recognize God teach that love and longing run through all beings, though in different degrees. All things, created and brought into being, draw from this vast sea of longing and bear witness to the oneness of the eternal Real. Each turns toward its own direction, seeking to reach it and to take from it the light of longing. The Qur'an points to this when it says, “There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise.”

Every being naturally seeks its own perfection: the goodness of its existence, which it receives from the First Good. It turns away from its own particular lack, which comes from matter and nonexistence. So every being has an inborn desire for the good. Goodness is loved for its own sake. For some beings, the good they love is the particular good suited to them; for others, it is the unqualified good—the Necessary Good, pure existence untouched by any lack or limitation. Each being finds what suits it pleasing and longs for it when it is absent. Love comes from what has been or will be received from the beloved. The greater the goodness and fullness of existence, the more it is loved and the stronger its love of the good.

The holy reality untouched by possibility or lack is the fullest good, and so is both the most beloved and the greatest lover. Since the divine attributes do not differ from His essence, love in Him is wholly one with His essence and existence. As for all other beings, either their existence is itself a form of love, or it comes from love.

Among created beings, the strongest love belongs to the active intellects. They receive the divine light directly, without bodily senses or imagination, and their activity brings about the lower things that follow. Next come the higher souls, which the active intellect brings from possibility into actuality and gives the power to form images, hold them, and rest in them. After these come the animal powers, and then the plant powers.

Each of these has a kind of worship suited to it, and imitates its higher source as far as it can. The worship of the higher beings will be explained in its proper place. Among lower beings, worship takes the form of yielding to what is higher, submitting to it, and passing its good on to what is lower.

Look at minerals: they accept impressions and shapes, and yield to melting and hammering. In this way they acknowledge their source and show their submission. The more readily a mineral can be shaped, and the brighter and more beautiful its form, the higher it is. The duller and less useful it is, like rock and stone, the lower it is.

Then look at plants. Their branches move to and fro in the breeze. A Persian verse compares a cypress tree swaying in the north wind to someone waving their hands and bowing. The plant praises and honors God as its leaves brush together and its branches move, and it gives its fruit to animals. A plant that resists this order and yields nothing useful is fit only for the fire.

Animals, in turn, serve human beings. They go where people lead them and carry loads to places that would otherwise be reached only with great hardship. Some animals, however, resist human service, like wild beasts and other untamed creatures.

Then there is human worship: people imitate the higher source through knowledge and action, understand what can be known, and rise beyond bodily concerns. Human beings have the power of speech, freedom to act, and a complete form. Their worship is the highest among earthly beings, and their knowledge the greatest among animals. But a person consumed by wrongdoing sinks below animals, plants, and minerals. Minerals accept the forms given to them, while that person refuses them. The tree bows and praises its Lord, while that person does not. Animals obey human beings, while that person does not obey or know their Lord. May God protect us from such heedlessness and forgetfulness.

People imitate the higher source through the thinking power, which understands general truths, and through practical reason, which governs the body and its powers. They use the senses to draw general ideas from particular things, and the imagination to help them think, so that they can reach what reason seeks. They restrain sexual desire—not for pleasure itself, but to imitate the First Cause by preserving the kinds of living things, especially the human kind. They train anger to face danger and take up arms to defend a just city and a good community. From the rational power come acts such as understanding intelligible things, readiness to face death, love of the next life, and longing to live near the Merciful Lord.

Understand these words in their true sense, not as invented poetry. Some of what I have said may sound like persuasion or rhetoric, but these are symbols; when examined closely, they lead to proof. In short, all things—intellects, souls, heavenly bodies, and earthly bodies—imitate the higher source. By their nature, they love and long to obey the First Cause. They have an inborn way of turning toward it and moving around it.

Avicenna says in several places in his Notes that earthly powers are like the souls of the heavens: what they seek through their actions lies above them. Nature and earthly souls do not move matter in order to produce something lower than themselves, such as a particular mixture or condition, even though these results necessarily follow. They move matter so that it may reach the best state possible for it and so imitate what is above it, just as the souls of the heavens move their bodies.

From this, a thoughtful reader can see that the goal of every mover, high or low, is the First Agent. The things it moves are directed toward Him, not toward what lies below them. This also explains the saying, “If the higher did not love, the lower would disappear.”

The same is true of what brings rest, such as the nature of the earth, and what brings motion, such as the natures of the heavens. What they seek is not something lower than themselves, such as a place. Their goal is to reach the best state possible for them, the state that suits them.

As the Second Teacher, Abu Nasr, says in The Gems: “The heavens pray through their turning, and the earth through its trembling. In everything we find a natural longing for what it loves and a tender desire for what it seeks.” Nothing is without such longing.

One of the people of insight says: “By my life, the heavens, in their swift turning and deep yearning, and the earth, in its stillness, are alike in this. The beauty of the First has reached them both: the heavens dance with joy, while the earth, overcome by what has come to it, lies stretched on the carpet. The pleasure of this vision has made them its servants; the sight of the Eternal’s kindness has taken their hearts.” As the verse says: “That is gratitude for boundless kindness; this is intoxication from the wine of longing.”

You may say: “Although a goal comes before an action in what it is, it must come after the action in existence, as its result. If God were both agent and goal, He would have to be prior to all possible beings and also later than them. The same thing would be both first of all and last of all.”

I reply: The goal comes after an action in existence only when the goal is something created. That does not apply when the goal is higher than creation. In acts of creation, the goal comes before what is brought about, in knowledge and in existence, though in different respects. God is first of all as the agent who causes everything, as we will prove. He is also the last of all as the goal and good toward which all things naturally turn and long, because He is goodness itself and the true beloved.

What makes Him the agent is His own essence. What makes Him the goal is that things proceed from Him in such a way that they naturally love Him: they preserve the perfections they already have and long to gain further perfections, so that they may resemble their source as far as possible. You now know the difference between a goal that belongs to a thing in itself and one that belongs to it only as a consequence.
